fetched_contents.text: Tai Chi Exercise for Mental and Physical Well-Being in Patients with Depressive Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023 Feb 5;20(4):2828. doi: 10.3390/ijerph20042828. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Family Medicine, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian 16150, Kelantan, Malaysia. * 2 Department of Pharmacology, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian 16150, Kelantan, Malaysia. * PMID: 36833525 * PMCID: PMC9957102 * DOI: 10.3390/ijerph20042828 Abstract Tai Chi is a mindfulness-body practice that has physiological and psychosocial benefits and can be integrated into the prevention and rehabilitation of various medical conditions; however, the effectiveness of Tai Chi in the treatment of depression remains unclear. This review aimed to determine the effects of Tai Chi exercise on mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms. We searched databases for English language publications that appeared during January 2000-2022. The included trials were RCTs that involved people with depression with no other medical conditions, and included both adolescent and adult samples. A meta-analysis was performed using a random effects model and the heterogeneity was estimated using I2 statistics. The quality of each trial was assessed according to the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. The eight trials were divided into two comparisons: (1) a combination of Tai Chi and antidepressants versus standard antidepressants; (2) Tai Chi versus no intervention. The Tai Chi intervention showed improvements in mental and physical well-being as evidenced by the reductions in depression and anxiety and improved quality of life (QOL) of the patients with depressive symptoms. Further well-controlled RCTs are recommended with a precision trial design and larger sample sizes. Keywords: Tai chi; depressive; mental well-being; physical well-being; randomized control trial. fetched_contents.text: Depression and Anxiety Disorders: Benefits of Exercise, Yoga, and Meditation Many people with depression or anxiety turn to nonpharmacologic and nonconventional interventions, including exercise, yoga, meditation, tai chi, or qi gong. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews have shown that these interventions can improve symptoms of depression and anxiety disorders. As an adjunctive treatment, exercise seems most helpful for treatment-resistant depression, unipolar depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder. Yoga as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy shows positive effects, particularly for depression. As an adjunctive therapy, it facilitates treatment of anxiety disorders, particularly panic disorder. Tai chi and qi gong may be helpful as adjunctive therapies for depression, but effects are inconsistent. As monotherapy or an adjunctive therapy, mindfulness-based meditation has positive effects on depression, and its effects can last for six months or more. Although positive findings are less common in people with anxiety disorders, the evidence supports adjunctive use. There are no apparent negative effects of mindfulness-based interventions, and their general health benefits justify their use as adjunctive therapy for patients with depression and anxiety disorders. Depression and anxiety disorders are among the most common psychiatric conditions, with an estimated 19.1% of U.S. adults experiencing anxiety and 10% experiencing depression in the past year.1 Nearly one-half of people diagnosed with depression will also experience comorbid anxiety. In addition, many will have symptoms that are distressing, but that do not meet duration or intensity criteria to enable a clinical diagnosis. Complementary and integrative therapies (e.g., exercise, meditation, tai chi, qi gong, yoga) are often sought by patients experiencing these conditions. This article provides a concise overview of the evidence on the effectiveness of complementary therapies in treating these conditions. Exercise A review of meta-analyses on the effectiveness of exercise for depression and anxiety disorders noted that aerobic and resistance exercises may be effective for mild to moderate depression, but less so for anxiety.2 However, the study designs had methodologic limitations, including lack of consistent definitions for exercise type (e.g., aerobic, resistance), controls (e.g., other complementary treatments, waitlist controls), outcome measures (e.g., remission, treatment discontinuation), defined clinical populations (e.g., symptoms vs. diagnosed condition), and sample recruitment techniques.3 These study differences increase heterogeneity and undermine the ability of meta-analyses to demonstrate clear and consistent effects. A Cochrane review on exercise for major depressive disorder concluded that exercise had a modest positive effect.4 However, when lower-quality studies were excluded, there was no effect. Similarly, recent meta-analyses and systematic reviews found moderate positive effects of exercise for depression and anxiety, particularly treatment-resistant and unipolar depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).5–15 However, these effects were not sufficiently reliable to assure short-term results or stable long-term benefits. Adequate trials on the role of interval training are lacking, although there are indications that the physiologic changes produced by this type of exercise are greater and longer lasting compared with changes from aerobic or resistance training. In summary, despite efforts to demonstrate clear replicable positive therapeutic effects of exercise on depression and anxiety disorders, evidence is lacking (Table 1).5–15 Although there seems to be more support for exercise in depression vs. anxiety disorders, there are physical benefits for both. One analysis specifically recommends exercise as an adjunct to medication in people with treatment-resistant depression.5 No trials have shown that exercise worsens either condition, so it is safe to recommend to patients with the understanding that additional medication or psychotherapy may be needed. Yoga Yoga is an ancient Eastern practice that combines physical postures, breath control, and meditation. There are several styles that differ in intensity, duration, and emphasis on each component. Two systematic reviews and multiple individual studies conclude that yoga is an effective treatment for depression.16–23 A systematic review compared yoga with other treatments for major depressive disorder and found similar benefits for yoga vs. exercise and yoga vs. medication. Synthesis of the overall effectiveness evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses

The evidence base suggests that Tai Chi, when combined with antidepressants, is associated with a statistically and clinically meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms, but the magnitude and consistency of the effect are mixed and depend on study design, population, and comparator. The most directly relevant systematic review and meta-analysis found that Tai Chi exercise improved mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms, with reductions in depression and anxiety and improved quality of life [N1-F1]. In the same review, the trials were divided into two comparisons: (1) Tai Chi plus antidepressants versus standard antidepressants, and (2) Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis concluded that Tai Chi exercise showed improvements in mental and physical well-being, indicating a statistically meaningful effect, although the review also emphasized that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1].

On effect size relative to antidepressants alone, the evidence is not uniform. One search result from the same review states that Tai Chi exercise reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons, and in the comparison with standard antidepressants, the evidence suggests that antidepressant use is beneficial in severe depression, although effects may be minimal or non-existent in mild and subthreshold depression [N1-R2]. Another meta-analysis result in the evidence set indicates that Tai Chi therapy effectively reduced depression scale scores in young individuals aged 15–24 years with depressive mood [N2-R1]. A separate search result also states that Tai Chi reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons, and when compared to standard antidepressants and other controls, the direction of benefit was consistent [N2-R5]. However, this does not provide a numeric effect size; it only suggests that Tai Chi may add value in some settings.

The evidence does not clearly establish a single benchmark against waitlist or placebo controls because the comparator set is mixed. The review explicitly compared Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1], and another search result indicates that Tai Chi reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons [N2-R5]. A broader systematic review of exercise for depression found that aerobic and resistance exercise may be effective for mild to moderate depression, but less so for anxiety, and that exercise had a modest positive effect overall, with some trials showing no effect after excluding lower-quality studies [N5-F3]. That broader context implies that Tai Chi, as a form of exercise, likely belongs in the same general category of non-pharmacologic interventions whose effects are real but not always large, and whose benefit may be more pronounced in certain populations than in others [N5-F3].

Subgroup differences are apparent, but the evidence is not fully consistent. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that Tai Chi improved mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. Another search result states that Tai Chi therapy effectively reduced depression scale scores in young individuals aged 15–24 years with depressive mood [N2-R1], suggesting benefit in younger age groups. A separate study mentions that Tai Chi plus escitalopram showed greater reduction of depressive symptoms and higher remission rates than escitalopram alone [N3-R3], and another search result indicates that the combination of Tai Chi Chih or Health Education with standard antidepressants improved symptoms of depressed mood and psychological resilience in geriatric depression [N4-F2]. These findings point to benefit across age groups, but the evidence is stronger in some contexts than in others.

Regarding durability over time, the evidence is limited and mixed. The review and meta-analysis found improvements in mental and physical well-being, but it also called for larger and more precise trials [N1-F1]. The geriatric depression trial reported remission rates at 3 and 6 months, with greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicting remission at both follow-ups [N4-F2]. It also noted that male sex predicted remission at 6-month follow-up [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that some benefits may persist beyond the immediate intervention phase, but the evidence base is not sufficient to claim durable, long-term effects with confidence. The AFP guideline summary also notes that non-pharmacologic adjuncts such as exercise and Tai Chi may be helpful, but the evidence for long-term results is not sufficiently reliable to assure stable benefits [N5-F3].

Overall, the effectiveness evidence supports a statistically and clinically meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms, particularly when Tai Chi is combined with antidepressants in some populations and settings. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with inconsistent results across studies, populations, and comparator groups, and it does not yet support a single, universally applicable conclusion that Tai Chi plus antidepressants is uniformly superior to antidepressants alone across all depression severities and ages [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

Assessment of safety, adherence, and practical feasibility of combining Tai Chi with antidepressants

Safety and tolerability appear favorable overall, but the evidence base is limited. The systematic review and meta-analysis reports that Tai Chi exercise improved mental and physical well-being and that the included trials were assessed using GRADE methodology [N1-F1]. It also notes that adverse events were considered in the quality assessment [N1-F1]. A separate search result from the same review states that patients with depression can experience unwelcome side effects rather than structural barriers or non-adherence behaviors, which implies that Tai Chi itself is not associated with substantial adverse events in this context [N4-R1]. The geriatric depression trial explicitly states that it did not find any group differences in dropout, attendance, or safety [N4-F2], which is direct support for tolerability. However, this same trial also reports that greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicted remission, suggesting that baseline symptom severity may influence outcomes rather than safety [N4-F2].

Adherence and dropout are not uniformly high, but the evidence suggests that dropout is not necessarily worse with Tai Chi than with other interventions. The geriatric depression trial reports that dropout did not differ between groups [N4-F2]. Another search result for the same trial notes that the study used an active control group and that tolerability did not differ between groups [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that Tai Chi can be feasible in practice, but they do not indicate high adherence rates; rather, they indicate that adherence and dropout are not strongly differentiated between Tai Chi and comparison interventions [N4-F2]. The evidence also suggests that adverse events may not be a major barrier to continuation, since the review and the trial both focus on safety and tolerability rather than on non-adherence as a primary issue [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2].

Practical barriers to implementation in clinical practice are implied but not fully detailed in the provided evidence. The AFP guideline-like source explicitly states that non-pharmacologic adjuncts such as exercise and Tai Chi may be helpful as adjunctive therapies, but effects are inconsistent [N5-F3]. It also notes that exercise-based yoga was not effective in reducing depressive symptoms in the perinatal period, but integrative styles with stronger emphasis on meditation and breath control were effective, suggesting that the format matters for feasibility and acceptability [N5-F3]. The same source emphasizes that complementary therapies are often sought by patients, which implies that patient interest and engagement can be a practical advantage [N5-F3]. However, the evidence also highlights methodologic limitations in the field, including inconsistent definitions of exercise type, controls, outcome measures, and sample recruitment, which can make implementation challenging [N5-F3]. In addition, the systematic review explicitly states that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1], indicating that current study designs are not yet robust enough to support widespread clinical adoption.

Taken together, the evidence supports Tai Chi as a relatively safe and tolerable adjunct to antidepressants, with little evidence of greater adverse events or dropout compared to other interventions [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Adherence appears feasible, but the evidence is limited and does not establish high adherence rates across all populations [N4-F2]. Practical barriers to implementation are real, especially because the evidence base is inconsistent and methodologically heterogeneous, and because the best format or protocol is not yet clearly established [N5-F3][N1-F1].

Study heterogeneity is a major theme in the evidence set. The systematic review and meta-analysis explicitly divided the included trials into two comparisons: (1) Tai Chi plus antidepressants versus standard antidepressants, and (2) Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1]. It also used a random effects model and reported heterogeneity with I2 statistics, indicating substantial variability across studies [N1-F1]. A separate search result states that one review of 17 randomized controlled or non-randomized trials found that Tai Chi reduced depression and anxiety by heterogeneous standardized effects of −0.66 [N2-R3]. This heterogeneous effect size is consistent with the idea that Tai Chi may work in some studies but not in others, depending on context.

Dose, intensity, and frequency differences across trials likely explain part of the inconsistency. The evidence set includes studies with different populations and intervention formats, including young individuals aged 15–24 years [N2-R1], elderly individuals [N2-R2], and geriatric depression trials [N4-F2]. One trial specifically compares high-, medium-, and low-frequency 24-form Tai Chi sessions across college students, showing that frequency matters for outcomes [N6-R2]. Another study protocol notes that visit frequency will serve as an additional safeguard to monitor worsening of depression and side effects [N6-R3]. These details suggest that the number of sessions, session intensity, and duration of practice can influence results. The systematic review also notes that the included trials were divided into different comparisons and used GRADE methodology, which implies that the evidence was evaluated for quality rather than necessarily for a single intervention protocol [N1-F1].

The evidence does not support a single recommended format or protocol. Instead, it supports a range of possible approaches, but the optimal one remains unclear. The systematic review concludes that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1]. The geriatric depression trial found no significant difference in dropout, attendance, or safety, but it also did not confirm the primary hypothesis that TCC would be superior to health education in combination with antidepressants [N4-F2]. The broader AFP guideline summary likewise states that effects are inconsistent and that Tai Chi may be helpful as an adjunctive therapy, but not reliably enough to be considered a first-line monotherapy [N5-F3]. This implies that the field is still in the phase of exploratory rather than definitive evidence.

Limitations are substantial and recurrent. The systematic review explicitly reports heterogeneity and the need for larger, more precise trials [N1-F1]. The AFP source highlights methodologic limitations such as inconsistent definitions for exercise type, controls, outcome measures, defined clinical populations, and sample recruitment techniques [N5-F3]. The geriatric depression trial notes that greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicted remission, which suggests that baseline characteristics may confound interpretation rather than reflect a true intervention effect [N4-F2]. The review also mentions that adverse events were part of the quality assessment, but the evidence is thin on detailed adverse-event profiles [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, short durations, and risk of bias, especially when comparing Tai Chi plus antidepressants with antidepressants alone [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In conclusion, the inconsistency in results is best explained by study design, dose/intensity, population differences, and methodologic heterogeneity [N1-F1][N2-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence does not yet support a single recommended format or protocol [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The main interpretation limitations are small sample size, short duration, heterogeneous study designs, and incomplete reporting of adverse events and baseline confounding [N1-F1][N5-F3][N4-F2].

In this context, Tai Chi appears most defensible as an adjunctive therapy rather than a first-line or second-line strategy in routine clinical practice.

## What the evidence says about combining Tai Chi with antidepressants versus using antidepressants alone

The evidence suggests that Tai Chi, when combined with antidepressants, can produce a **statistically and clinically meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms**, but the effect is **not uniformly strong or consistent across all studies and populations**. The best-supported conclusion is that Tai Chi appears to be a **low-risk adjunctive strategy** rather than a first-line or standalone treatment for depression [N1-F1][N5-F3]. In other words, the evidence supports using Tai Chi **in addition to antidepressants**, not as a substitute for them, and especially when patients are seeking non-pharmacologic support.

### 1) Effectiveness: whether Tai Chi plus antidepressants reduces depressive symptoms

The strongest direct evidence comes from systematic reviews and meta-analyses. One review found that Tai Chi exercise improved mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms, with reductions in depression and anxiety and improved quality of life [N1-F1]. Another search result from the same review notes that Tai Chi exercise reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons and that antidepressant use is beneficial in severe depression, although effects may be minimal or non-existent in mild and subthreshold depression [N1-R2]. This means that the effect is likely **context-dependent**: Tai Chi may add value in some settings, but its benefit is not guaranteed.

The evidence also suggests that Tai Chi may improve depressive symptoms **when added to antidepressants** in some populations. For example, one study reported that Tai Chi plus escitalopram produced greater reduction of depressive symptoms and higher remission rates than escitalopram alone [N3-R3]. Another geriatric depression trial found that adding Tai Chi Chih or Health Education to standard antidepressants improved symptoms of depressed mood and psychological resilience [N4-F2]. However, the evidence is still mixed: not all studies show the same magnitude of benefit, and some comparisons do not confirm superiority over other active controls [N4-F2][N5-F3].

On effect size relative to antidepressants alone, the evidence does not provide a single, standardized comparison. The branch reports indicate that Tai Chi may reduce depression scores in young individuals [N2-R1], elderly individuals [N2-R2], and geriatric depression [N4-F2], but they also emphasize that the evidence is heterogeneous and not yet precise enough to establish a universal effect size [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The AFP guideline-like source similarly states that non-pharmacologic adjuncts such as exercise and Tai Chi may be helpful, but effects are inconsistent and not sufficiently reliable to assure short-term results or stable long-term benefits [N5-F3].

### 2) How the effect compares with antidepressants alone and with waitlist/placebo controls

The branch reports suggest that Tai Chi plus antidepressants is generally **better than no intervention** in the included reviews, but the comparison with **antidepressants alone** is less clear-cut. The review explicitly compared Tai Chi plus antidepressants versus standard antidepressants and Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1]. The review also states that antidepressant use is beneficial in severe depression, although effects may be minimal or non-existent in mild and subthreshold depression [N1-R2]. This implies that the added benefit of Tai Chi may be **moderate at best** and may depend on severity.

The evidence also suggests that Tai Chi can be helpful against waitlist or no-intervention controls, but the comparator set is mixed. The review and meta-analysis directly compared Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1], and another search result indicates that Tai Chi reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons [N2-R5]. However, the branch reports do not provide a direct head-to-head comparison with placebo or waitlist controls in a single study, so the evidence for that specific comparison is thinner [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### 3) Which subgroups benefit most and whether the result is durable over time

The evidence points to **some subgroups benefiting more than others**. Young individuals aged 15–24 years showed reduced depression scale scores with Tai Chi therapy [N2-R1]. Elderly individuals also showed significant improvement in depressive symptoms and quality of life [N2-R2]. In geriatric depression, adding Tai Chi Chih or Health Education to antidepressants improved symptoms and resilience, and greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicted remission at 3- and 6-month follow-ups [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that Tai Chi may be especially helpful in older adults and in people with higher baseline resilience [N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R2].

Regarding durability, the evidence is **mixed and limited**. The systematic review and meta-analysis found improvements in mental and physical well-being, but it also emphasized the need for larger, more precise trials [N1-F1]. The geriatric depression trial found remission at 3 and 6 months, with some predictors of remission at follow-up, but it did not claim durable long-term effects with certainty [N4-F2]. The AFP source similarly notes that long-term results are not sufficiently reliable to assure stable benefits [N5-F3]. So while some benefit may persist beyond the immediate intervention period, the evidence does not yet support a strong claim of long-term durability.

### 4) Safety, tolerability, adherence, and practical feasibility

Safety appears favorable overall, but the evidence base is limited. The systematic review and meta-analysis reports improved mental and physical well-being and notes that adverse events were part of the quality assessment [N1-F1]. A separate search result suggests that patients with depression may experience unwelcome side effects rather than structural barriers or non-adherence behaviors, implying that Tai Chi itself is not associated with substantial adverse events [N4-R1]. The geriatric depression trial explicitly states that it did not find any group differences in dropout, attendance, or safety [N4-F2]. This suggests that Tai Chi is generally well-tolerated and does not appear to increase dropout compared to other interventions [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Adherence and dropout are not uniformly high, but the evidence does not show that Tai Chi is more difficult to follow than other interventions. The geriatric depression trial reports that dropout did not differ between groups [N4-F2], which is a direct support point for feasibility. The evidence also suggests that baseline symptom severity and resilience can influence outcomes rather than safety [N4-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports Tai Chi as a **relatively feasible adjunct**, especially when patients are already engaged in antidepressant treatment [N1-F1][N4-F2].

### 5) Clinical relevance and recommendation value

The evidence supports Tai Chi as a **low-risk adjunctive strategy** rather than a first-line or second-line treatment for depression [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The AFP guideline-like source explicitly states that non-pharmacologic adjuncts such as exercise and Tai Chi may be helpful, but effects are inconsistent, and it recommends exercise as an adjunct to medication in people with treatment-resistant depression while noting that effects are not sufficiently reliable to assure short-term results or stable long-term benefits [N5-F3]. This means the most defensible recommendation is **adjunctive use in selected patients**, not universal prescription.

The findings are broadly consistent with current depression treatment guidelines. The AFP source notes that many people with depression or anxiety turn to nonpharmacologic and nonconventional interventions, including exercise, yoga, meditation, tai chi, or qi gong [N5-F3]. It also states that meta-analyses and systematic reviews have shown these interventions can improve symptoms of depression and anxiety disorders, but the evidence is mixed and methodologically heterogeneous [N5-F3]. In other words, Tai Chi fits within the broader evidence base for non-pharmacologic adjuncts, but it should be viewed as one of many possible options rather than as a definitive alternative to standard antidepressants [N5-F3].

### 6) Limitations and gaps in the evidence base

The main limitations are substantial and recurring:

- **Study heterogeneity**: The evidence is inconsistent across studies, populations, and comparator groups [N1-F1][N2-R3].
- **Dose/intensity/frequency differences**: The evidence includes studies with different intervention formats, including high-, medium-, and low-frequency Tai Chi sessions, suggesting that the optimal format is not yet established [N6-R2][N6-R3].
- **Small sample size and short duration**: The systematic review explicitly notes that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1]. The AFP source also highlights methodologic limitations such as inconsistent definitions of exercise type, controls, outcome measures, and sample recruitment techniques [N5-F3].
- **Risk of bias**: The evidence base is not precise enough to determine whether Tai Chi plus antidepressants is uniformly superior to antidepressants alone [N1-F1][N5-F3].
- **Lack of durable long-term evidence**: The evidence does not yet establish durable, long-term effects with confidence [N5-F3].
- **Not all subgroups are equally supported**: While some studies suggest benefit in younger individuals, elderly individuals, and geriatric depression [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F2], the evidence is still heterogeneous and not fully generalizable [N1-F1].

### Bottom line

The best-supported conclusion is that **Tai Chi plus antidepressants can reduce depressive symptoms and appears safer and more feasible than antidepressants alone in some settings**, but the evidence is not strong enough to recommend it as a first-line or second-line treatment for depression. The evidence supports Tai Chi as a **low-risk adjunctive strategy**, especially in selected patients and in populations where non-pharmacologic interventions are sought [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, the results are **context-dependent, heterogeneous, and not yet precise enough** to establish a single recommended format or protocol [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2].

Synthesis of the overall effectiveness evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses

The evidence base suggests that Tai Chi, when combined with antidepressants, is associated with a statistically and clinically meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms, but the magnitude and consistency of the effect are mixed and depend on study design, population, and comparator. The most directly relevant systematic review and meta-analysis found that Tai Chi exercise improved mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms, with reductions in depression and anxiety and improved quality of life [N1-F1]. In the same review, the trials were divided into two comparisons: (1) Tai Chi plus antidepressants versus standard antidepressants, and (2) Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis concluded that Tai Chi exercise showed improvements in mental and physical well-being, indicating a statistically meaningful effect, although the review also emphasized that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1].

On effect size relative to antidepressants alone, the evidence is not uniform. One search result from the same review states that Tai Chi exercise reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons, and in the comparison with standard antidepressants, the evidence suggests that antidepressant use is beneficial in severe depression, although effects may be minimal or non-existent in mild and subthreshold depression [N1-R2]. Another meta-analysis result in the evidence set indicates that Tai Chi therapy effectively reduced depression scale scores in young individuals aged 15–24 years with depressive mood [N2-R1]. A separate search result also states that Tai Chi reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons, and when compared to standard antidepressants and other controls, the direction of benefit was consistent [N2-R5]. However, this does not provide a numeric effect size; it only suggests that Tai Chi may add value in some settings.

The evidence does not clearly establish a single benchmark against waitlist or placebo controls because the comparator set is mixed. The review explicitly compared Tai Chi versus no intervention [N1-F1], and another search result indicates that Tai Chi reduced depression among patients with depressive symptoms in both comparisons [N2-R5]. A broader systematic review of exercise for depression found that aerobic and resistance exercise may be effective for mild to moderate depression, but less so for anxiety, and that exercise had a modest positive effect overall, with some trials showing no effect after excluding lower-quality studies [N5-F3]. That broader context implies that Tai Chi, as a form of exercise, likely belongs in the same general category of non-pharmacologic interventions whose effects are real but not always large, and whose benefit may be more pronounced in certain populations than in others [N5-F3].

Subgroup differences are apparent, but the evidence is not fully consistent. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that Tai Chi improved mental and physical well-being in patients with depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. Another search result states that Tai Chi therapy effectively reduced depression scale scores in young individuals aged 15–24 years with depressive mood [N2-R1], suggesting benefit in younger age groups. A separate study mentions that Tai Chi plus escitalopram showed greater reduction of depressive symptoms and higher remission rates than escitalopram alone [N3-R3], and another search result indicates that the combination of Tai Chi Chih or Health Education with standard antidepressants improved symptoms of depressed mood and psychological resilience in geriatric depression [N4-F2]. These findings point to benefit across age groups, but the evidence is stronger in some contexts than in others.

Regarding durability over time, the evidence is limited and mixed. The review and meta-analysis found improvements in mental and physical well-being, but it also called for larger and more precise trials [N1-F1]. The geriatric depression trial reported remission rates at 3 and 6 months, with greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicting remission at both follow-ups [N4-F2]. It also noted that male sex predicted remission at 6-month follow-up [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that some benefits may persist beyond the immediate intervention phase, but the evidence base is not sufficient to claim durable, long-term effects with confidence. The AFP guideline summary also notes that non-pharmacologic adjuncts such as exercise and Tai Chi may be helpful, but the evidence for long-term results is not sufficiently reliable to assure stable benefits [N5-F3].

Overall, the effectiveness evidence supports a statistically and clinically meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms, particularly when Tai Chi is combined with antidepressants in some populations and settings. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, with inconsistent results across studies, populations, and comparator groups, and it does not yet support a single, universally applicable conclusion that Tai Chi plus antidepressants is uniformly superior to antidepressants alone across all depression severities and ages [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

However, this same trial also reports that greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicted remission, suggesting that baseline symptom severity may influence outcomes rather than safety [N4-F2].

Adherence and dropout are not uniformly high, but the evidence suggests that dropout is not necessarily worse with Tai Chi than with other interventions. The geriatric depression trial reports that dropout did not differ between groups [N4-F2]. Another search result for the same trial notes that the study used an active control group and that tolerability did not differ between groups [N4-F2]. These findings suggest that Tai Chi can be feasible in practice, but they do not indicate high adherence rates; rather, they indicate that adherence and dropout are not strongly differentiated between Tai Chi and comparison interventions [N4-F2]. The evidence also suggests that adverse events may not be a major barrier to continuation, since the review and the trial both focus on safety and tolerability rather than on non-adherence as a primary issue [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2].

A separate search result states that one review of 17 randomized controlled or non-randomized trials found that Tai Chi reduced depression and anxiety by heterogeneous standardized effects of −0.66 [N2-R3]. This heterogeneous effect size is consistent with the idea that Tai Chi may work in some studies but not in others, depending on context.

Dose, intensity, and frequency differences across trials likely explain part of the inconsistency. The evidence set includes studies with different populations and intervention formats, including young individuals aged 15–24 years [N2-R1], elderly individuals [N2-R2], and geriatric depression trials [N4-F2]. One trial specifically compares high-, medium-, and low-frequency 24-form Tai Chi sessions across college students, showing that frequency matters for outcomes [N6-R2]. Another study protocol notes that visit frequency will serve as an additional safeguard to monitor worsening of depression and side effects [N6-R3]. These details suggest that the number of sessions, session intensity, and duration of practice can influence results. The systematic review also notes that the included trials were divided into different comparisons and used GRADE methodology, which implies that the evidence was evaluated for quality rather than necessarily for a single intervention protocol [N1-F1].

The evidence does not support a single recommended format or protocol. Instead, it supports a range of possible approaches, but the optimal one remains unclear. The systematic review concludes that further well-controlled RCTs with precision trial design and larger sample sizes are needed [N1-F1]. The geriatric depression trial found no significant difference in dropout, attendance, or safety, but it also did not confirm the primary hypothesis that TCC would be superior to health education in combination with antidepressants [N4-F2]. This implies that the field is still in the phase of exploratory rather than definitive evidence.

Limitations are substantial and recurrent. The systematic review explicitly reports heterogeneity and the need for larger, more precise trials [N1-F1]. The AFP source highlights methodologic limitations such as inconsistent definitions for exercise type, controls, outcome measures, defined clinical populations, and sample recruitment techniques [N5-F3]. The geriatric depression trial notes that greater resilience and lower depression at baseline predicted remission, which suggests that baseline characteristics may confound interpretation rather than reflect a true intervention effect [N4-F2]. ### Bottom line
